operationalization: Within well-sampled formations, count morphologically intermediate specimens between successive allied species and record whether close forms from different levels are given separate species names. A large roster of named intermediates inside single formations would undermine the scarcity expectation.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil occurrences, formation-level stratigraphy, and the species names assigned to them

obstacles: A few has no numeric cutoff, so only an extreme abundance of intermediates would count against the expectation.
Ranking close morphs as species is a taxonomic decision, so the second clause partly describes practice rather than an independent biological fact.
Single formations rarely preserve continuous populations finely enough to see transitional series.
rationale: Occurrence records and species names are public, but morphological intermediacy is not a field in those databases and has to be assembled from clade-by-clade studies. The scarcity half is elastic, and the naming half is entangled with how palaeontologists already define species. Existing data can examine a few well-studied formations, which is a restricted slice of the stated scope.

operationalization: Compare present first-appearance dates of genera and families with the dates in earlier compilations, and with the level at which each group becomes diverse. Continued discovery of substantially older fossils supports the claim; first appearances that stay fixed after dense sampling of older rocks count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Stratigraphic ranges and the history of when occurrences were entered, for shifts in first appearances

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: Rock-package ages and volumes used to judge whether older intervals have actually been sampled

obstacles: A continued absence of older fossils can be attributed to remaining gaps in the record.
Rock availability and collecting effort are uneven below the horizons where a group is already known.
rationale: First appearances and the sampling of older strata are standard, downloadable variables, and a small team can measure how far ranges have moved backward. Marine shelly groups are well enough covered to test the general pattern; soft-bodied and terrestrial groups are not. The test is informative once collecting effort is included, with the residual limit that an absence can still be blamed on preservation.

operationalization: For clades that gained a novel habit such as flight, measure the time from the oldest stem fossil to the appearance of many divergent, geographically widespread subclades. A long prelude and then a short global radiation would support the claim; diversification spread evenly across the whole interval would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: First occurrences and geographic spread of pterosaurs, birds, bats, and flying insects

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: Published divergence times for the radiations that followed those origins

obstacles: The acquisition of the new habit itself is rarely fossilized, so the long prelude is weakly constrained.
Comparatively short needs an external yardstick, and clock dates and fossil dates often disagree.
Only a few novel habits have both a fossil origin and a resolved radiation.
rationale: Fossil occurrences and published timetrees can time the radiations of bats, birds, and pterosaurs, which is the testable core for a few cases. The preceding long evolution of the habit is mostly unrecorded, so that half of the statement stays thin. Results for flight do not automatically extend to every new way of life.

operationalization: Compare the radiometric duration before Darwin's lowest fossiliferous strata, mapped to the base of the Cambrian, with the duration from that horizon to the present, and score whether fossils or biomarkers show widespread life through the earlier interval. A shorter pre-Cambrian span, or a span lacking evidence of life, would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: International Commission on Stratigraphy
candidate_datasets.role: Geologic time scale used to compare the pre-Cambrian and Cambrian-to-Recent intervals

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Precambrian and early Phanerozoic fossil occurrences as evidence of pre-Silurian life

obstacles: Lowest Silurian in the 1859 text has to be aligned with the modern base of the Cambrian.
Swarmed is qualitative, and the early record is mostly microbial and concentrated in particular facies.
rationale: The duration comparison is a direct arithmetic use of the geologic time scale, and Precambrian fossils are public even though they are sparse. The mapping from Darwin's Silurian onto the Cambrian is historically standard. Abundance of life is less sharp than the time comparison, but the existence of a long earlier biosphere is decidable with current compilations.

operationalization: Compare Silurian-to-Recent paleogeographic reconstructions with the present positions of continents and ocean basins. Opening or closure of major ocean basins, or large lateral shifts of continental crust, would refute long-term stability of those areas.

candidate_datasets.name: EarthByte
candidate_datasets.role: Plate-tectonic reconstructions of continent and ocean positions since the Paleozoic

candidate_datasets.name: GPlates
candidate_datasets.role: Open plate model and software for measuring displacement of continental crust through time

obstacles: Paleozoic plate reconstructions are less precise than Mesozoic and Cenozoic ones.
Ocean crust older than the Jurassic has been subducted, so ancient ocean positions are inferred from continental margins.
rationale: Published plate models directly record whether oceans and continents stayed in their present areas. The displacements involved, such as the opening of the Atlantic, are large relative to reconstruction uncertainty. Paleozoic detail is coarser, but it is still sufficient to confirm or refute stability since the earliest Silurian.

operationalization: In terrestrial and marine occurrence data, test whether first appearances are spread across successive time bins or clustered in the same short horizons. A staggered sequence supports successive appearance; repeated pulses of many unrelated first appearances, beyond sampling spikes, would challenge it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Sampled first appearances of marine and terrestrial taxa through Phanerozoic bins

obstacles: Geological stages are coarser than one-after-another within a formation.
The record is mostly genera, so species-level succession is a proxy.
The terrestrial record is much patchier than the marine record, and bedding-scale collecting spikes imitate simultaneous origin.
rationale: Origination series are a standard Paleobiology Database analysis and can be run quickly with sampling standardization. They resolve genus-level marine turnover, especially in the Cenozoic, and leave species-level and terrestrial succession weakly covered. Bin length and sampling spikes keep the test from isolating truly simultaneous batches.

operationalization: Estimate taxonomic turnover, or morphological rate where character data exist, separately by class and by genus, and test whether those rates are equal. A wide spread of rates would support the claim; statistically indistinguishable rates across classes would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Origination and extinction rates computed separately by class and genus

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Character matrices for morphological rates in the subsets of clades that have them

obstacles: Classes differ in preservation and in how finely taxonomists split them, which can imitate rate differences.
Direct morphological rates exist for far fewer groups than taxonomic turnover does.
rationale: Unequal rates are a direct, confirm-or-refute contrast, and class-level marine turnover is downloadable and analyzable with ordinary subsampling. Taxonomic practice can inflate differences, but that bias is measurable by comparing sampling-standardized rates. Morphological rates add a check for a subset of clades and are not required for the taxonomic reading of the claim.

operationalization: Compare per-lineage origination, extinction, or morphological-change rates for terrestrial versus marine taxa over the same Phanerozoic intervals, after sampling standardization. Faster terrestrial change would support the claim; equal or slower terrestrial change would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Environment-coded occurrences for comparing terrestrial and marine turnover

candidate_datasets.name: NOW fossil mammal database
candidate_datasets.role: Cenozoic land-mammal occurrences as the best-sampled terrestrial record

obstacles: Land fossils are rarer and more episodic than marine shells, which moves apparent rates even when biological rates are similar.
Environment is incompletely coded, and many important terrestrial groups have little pre-Cenozoic record.
rationale: The land-versus-sea contrast maps cleanly onto environment-coded turnover, and both marine occurrences and Cenozoic land mammals are public. Coverage is adequate for a Cenozoic mammal-versus-marine comparison and poor for the full Phanerozoic scope. Preservation differences push in the same direction as the claim often enough that a raw rate gap would not be decisive.

operationalization: Inspect species ranges for a disappearance followed by a later occurrence of the same species after a gap too long to be one continuous population. A later population that must be a new origin of the identical form would refute the claim; gaps explained by sampling would leave it standing.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Species-level stratigraphic ranges and Lazarus gaps

obstacles: Incomplete sampling creates gaps that look like disappearance and return.
Identical form is unstable where fossils are feature-poor and species names are applied inconsistently.
rationale: Stratigraphic ranges are public and can be screened for reappearances in weeks. Most gaps are sampling artefacts, so an apparent return rarely forces a true re-origin of the same species. The analysis can clear many Lazarus cases and still cannot certify that an identical form has never arisen twice.

operationalization: Measure internal gaps in genus and family ranges and ask whether any group is genuinely absent from a well-sampled interval and then resumes. Persistent occurrence at low density would support continuity; a well-sampled absence followed by return of the same group would challenge it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Genus and family ranges and collection counts used to judge whether gaps are sampled

obstacles: If groups are treated as clades, continuity through time is close to a definition and the test loses force.
Lazarus gaps from uneven collecting dominate apparent disappearances and returns.
rationale: Genus and family ranges are directly downloadable and better populated than species ranges. The empirical pattern of stratigraphic continuity can be described for marine invertebrates. Sampling gaps, and the shift from Darwin's morphological groups to monophyletic taxa, keep a clean refutation rare.

operationalization: For genera and families with long records, fit diversity through time and classify paths as a gradual rise to a single maximum and then a gradual fall, versus abrupt, flat, or multi-peaked paths. The claim holds if the unimodal gradual path is the statistical rule after sampling standardization.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Sampling-standardized genus and family richness trajectories through the Phanerozoic

obstacles: Pull of the Recent and uneven rock volume distort raw diversity curves.
Range-edge effects can make a trajectory look tapered at both ends.
rationale: Clade richness through time is a standard product of open occurrence data, and the unimodal pattern is a specific shape that can fail. Marine genera and families have the coverage the scope asks for; species-within-genus counts are thinner. Known sampling biases are serious and are also the subject of routine corrections, so the predominant shape is decidable.

operationalization: Compare last-appearance timing of species and genera across regions, and the share of extinctions that fall in globally correlated short intervals versus staggered regional losses. Globally synchronous removal as the usual pattern would challenge the claim; regionally staggered losses outside those intervals would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Last appearances with paleocoordinates, for regional versus global extinction timing

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: Independent section ages used to align regional disappearances

obstacles: The Signor-Lipps effect smears an abrupt extinction backward so that it looks gradual.
Geographic coverage is too thin to follow most individual species from place to place.
rationale: Global event horizons versus staggered regional last appearances are measurable with occurrence data and independent section ages. Methods that put confidence intervals on last appearances reduce, without removing, the tendency of incomplete ranges to look gradual. The usual pattern across the later record can be scored even though place-by-place paths exist only for better-sampled groups.

operationalization: For each genus or family, compare the time from first appearance to the diversity peak with the time from the peak to last appearance. Systematically longer declines would support the claim; equal or shorter declines, once sampling bias is accounted for, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Clade richness curves used to time the rise and the fall of groups

obstacles: The Signor-Lipps effect lengthens apparent declines, which is the same direction as the claim.
How a group is delimited changes the measured durations of its rise and fall.
rationale: Rise and fall durations are computable from public richness curves for many marine groups. The principal sampling bias manufactures slower-looking extinctions, so an uncorrected asymmetry would not distinguish the claim from an artefact. Corrected analyses can be done for well-sampled clades and remain ambiguous for the general case.

operationalization: Compare occupancy or occurrence counts in the interval before last appearance with counts for species that survive the same interval. A drop confined to the species that are about to disappear would support the claim; extinction from high occupancy would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence counts in the bins preceding last appearances

candidate_datasets.name: Neotoma Paleoecology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Quaternary abundance trajectories for species that later went extinct

obstacles: The Signor-Lipps effect produces a spurious decline in records before the last appearance.
Most fossil collections record presence, so rarity is occupancy rather than population size.
Historical cases of human extermination are documented piecemeal and are not one abundance series.
rationale: Pre-extinction occupancy is a clear variable, and both fossil occurrences and Quaternary paleoecological counts exist. The classic sampling bias creates exactly the decline the claim predicts, so an uncorrected result has little discriminating power. Neotoma and a few historical series can test true abundance for a recent subset.

operationalization: Compare sampling-standardized origination and extinction counts, and the trend in standing diversity, through the Cenozoic and other later Phanerozoic intervals. Matched gains and losses with flat diversity would support a balance; a sustained rise in diversity would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Sampling-standardized global diversity, origination, and extinction for later Phanerozoic intervals

obstacles: Different standardizations still disagree about whether later diversity is flat or rising.
Later geological periods is an elastic interval, and global species richness is not observed directly.
rationale: Origination, extinction, and standing diversity are the right variables and are already compiled. The scientific disagreement that remains is largely about sampling and rock volume, which means the same public data do not yet yield one decisive balance test. A restricted marine, genus-level version of the question is analyzable now.

operationalization: In clades that have both a species-level phylogeny and fossil occurrences, test whether the closest relatives disappear sooner after a species originates than more distant members of the family. Preferential loss of the parent and congeners, beyond shared habitat, would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Extinction timing of fossil species that can be placed against their relatives

candidate_datasets.name: NOW fossil mammal database
candidate_datasets.role: Cenozoic mammal occurrences for groups that also have species-level trees

obstacles: Parent and descendant are rarely separable from sister species in the fossil record.
Close relatives share climates and habitats, so they can disappear together without competition between them.
Species-level trees tied to occurrences cover only a few groups.
rationale: The pattern of which relatives disappear first is measurable only where a phylogeny and a fossil record coincide, a small part of the stated scope. Causation by competition is a further inference that co-extinction under a shared environment also predicts. A small team could run the test for planktonic foraminifera or mammals and would not cover genera in general.

operationalization: Date marine faunal turnovers with radiometric, paleomagnetic, or chemostratigraphic ages and compare their timing across paleocontinents. Turnover coincident within a geological stage worldwide would support the claim; multi-stage diachrony as the usual pattern would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Marine occurrences with paleocoordinates for cross-regional faunal comparison

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: Section ages independent of the fossil lists being correlated

candidate_datasets.name: International Commission on Stratigraphy
candidate_datasets.role: Stage framework and radiometric ages for judging what counts as simultaneous

obstacles: Correlation that uses the fossils themselves makes simultaneity circular.
Independent dates are dense in some periods and sparse in others.
rationale: Cross-regional marine turnover is densely recorded, and independent age frameworks exist so the test need not use the fossils as their own clock. Agreement within a stage is a concrete criterion matching the broad geological sense of the claim. Coverage is stronger for shelly and microfossil faunas than for every marine group.

operationalization: For fossil genera binned by age, measure taxonomic or morphological distance to the nearest living relatives and test whether that distance increases with age. No age trend, or ancient forms as similar to living ones as younger fossils are, would refute the general rule.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Age of fossil genera and whether those genera and families still have living members

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Character matrices for morphological distance to living relatives in covered clades

obstacles: Taxonomic rank is a coarse stand-in for amount of difference.
Living-fossil exceptions are expected under a general rule and have to be scored as exceptions, which softens the test.
Character matrices cover a subset of clades.
rationale: Age versus membership in extant genera and families is directly tabulated and is the comparison Darwin's taxonomic language supports. A regression of distance on age can be run on occurrence data in weeks, with morphospace as a check in covered clades. Living fossils and rank conventions reduce sharpness without making the age trend untestable.

operationalization: In character matrices, measure morphological distances among living orders and families with fossils excluded and again with fossils included. Fossils that sit in the gaps and shrink those distances would support the claim; fossils that only repeat living clusters would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Published character matrices that include both fossil and living members of a clade

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic placement of extinct genera relative to living orders and families

obstacles: Matrices cover some clades well and most of life poorly.
The characters that define the gaps are also the characters used to place the fossils.
Harmonizing many matrices into one analysis takes months.
rationale: Gap-filling is measurable as a reduction in morphological distance once fossils are added, and public matrices exist for many vertebrate and invertebrate clades. They do not cover all organisms, and the placement of fossils is not fully independent of the gaps. The analysis is realistic for several major groups and not for the universal scope.

operationalization: For pairs of groups with a long later history, compare character distances among their early members with distances among their living members. Early members as distinct as living members, or more so, would refute a backward approach between the groups.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Time-sliced character matrices for distances within and between allied groups

obstacles: Suitable matrices exist for a minority of the group pairs in the scope.
Loss of soft tissues can make older fossils look more alike than the living animals were.
rationale: The prediction is a directional comparison of distances through time and is well posed wherever a matrix spans both ancient and living members. Those matrices are public but scattered, and a global pair-of-groups test would take substantial harmonization. Taphonomic loss of characters is a real bias toward the predicted pattern, so results have to be restricted to characters preserved in both ages.

operationalization: Compute faunal similarity between geological stages and test whether similarity falls as the time gap grows, and whether each stage is compositionally intermediate between the stages before and after it. Similarity unrelated to temporal proximity would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Genus occurrences by stage for faunal similarity versus time separation

obstacles: Neighbouring formations can share facies, so environmental tracking imitates temporal relatedness.
Uneven sampling by stage changes measured similarity.
rationale: Faunal similarity against time separation is a standard calculation on public occurrence data and can be finished in weeks. The intermediacy clause is the same matrix read along the time axis. Facies and sampling are manageable by restricting comparisons to similar environments and by subsampling, and they do not erase a large decay of similarity with time.

operationalization: The stated test is a competition, under a similar climate, between an extinct fauna or flora and a living one. No existing observation records the winner of that encounter, and modern invasions or trait trends change the contrast into a different question.
obstacles: Extinct species cannot be placed in competition with living ones.
Competitive superiority is not a variable stored in occurrence or trait data without replacing the claim.
rationale: The statement is a counterfactual about a meeting that the fossil record does not contain. Any real pattern of replacement is compatible with later forms being competitively superior and with later forms merely being different. Proxies require a substantial reinterpretation, so they do not resolve the claim as stated.

operationalization: For late Cenozoic mammals, birds, and molluscs, compare the relatedness of each region's fossils to that region's living fauna and to the living faunas of other regions. Fossils systematically closest to the local living biota would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: NOW fossil mammal database
candidate_datasets.role: Late Cenozoic land-mammal occurrences by continent for comparison with living faunas

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Regional fossil occurrences of mammals, birds, and molluscs

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Living species distributions used as the successor faunas

obstacles: Later dispersal and extinction can erase an older regional succession.
Similar climates can produce convergent resemblance that has to be separated with phylogenetic affinity.
rationale: Regional fossil lists and living distributions are both public, and phylogenetic relatedness separates local succession from climatic convergence. Mammals in the later Tertiary are well enough covered for a direct test; birds and molluscs are spottier. The comparison is a standard biogeographic analysis on existing downloads.

operationalization: Partition compositional dissimilarity among the world's regions into a climate component and a regional component, including matched southern temperate belts. If climate distance accounts for which regions share their biotas, the claim fails.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Species occurrences by region for compositional similarity

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim
candidate_datasets.role: Climate layers used as the physical-conditions predictor

obstacles: Occurrence data are denser in some countries, which can exaggerate regional differences.
Present climate omits the conditions lineages experienced in the past.
rationale: Community dissimilarity, climate distance, and region identity are standard variables in two open global sources. Variation partitioning can be run for plants and vertebrates at the regional scale the claim uses. Sampling bias is real and is handled by restricting the test to well-sampled cells and higher taxa.

operationalization: Measure taxonomic turnover across oceans, mountains, deserts, and large rivers, and test whether turnover rises with barrier age and impermeability after climate is controlled. No residual association between barriers and biotic difference would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Distributions used to measure turnover across barriers

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim
candidate_datasets.role: Climate covariates so barrier effects are not confused with climate breaks

candidate_datasets.name: EarthByte
candidate_datasets.role: Ages of ocean basins and major tectonic barriers

obstacles: Barriers often sit on climate breaks, so the two predictors are collinear.
Barrier age is well known for ocean basins and poorly known for many rivers and deserts.
rationale: Distributions, climate, and ocean-basin ages are public and enough to test whether major barriers track biotic differences beyond climate. The age-and-impermeability gradient is cleanest for oceans and mountain systems and weaker for rivers. Collinearity lowers the precision of the split and does not remove the test.

operationalization: Compare phylogenetic similarity within a continent or sea, across habitats, with similarity between different continents that share a habitat. Habitat matches across continents as close as within-continent relatives would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Species composition within continents, oceans, and habitats

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogeny used to score relatedness rather than shared species names alone

obstacles: Many branches still lack a complete tree, so some comparisons stay at the level of shared genera.
Recent human introductions blur regional affinity if they are left in the lists.
rationale: Within-region relatedness versus between-region habitat matching is a standard phylogenetic beta-diversity contrast, and both occurrences and a synthetic tree are public. Vertebrates and seed plants are sufficiently covered; many invertebrates are not. Filtering introductions is routine and leaves a decisive comparison for the major regions.

operationalization: Ask whether regional biotas form phylogenetic clusters on molecular trees built independently of the morphological resemblance naturalists scored, and whether regional trait differences exceed what the physical environment predicts. Shared ancestry can be assessed that way; attributing the differences mainly to natural selection remains weakly separated from other causes.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Synthetic phylogeny for clustering of regional biotas

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Sequences underlying molecular trees that are independent of morphological affinity

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Geographic ranges joined to the trees

obstacles: A tree built from the same traits that display the affinity would make the inheritance test circular.
Selection, drift, and direct effects of the environment are not separated by present distributions.
Joint phylogenetic and geographic coverage is partial for the full living and fossil scope.
rationale: Molecular relatedness of regional faunas and floras is testable with open trees and sequences, and that test is independent of the morphological pattern it is meant to explain. The further split between natural selection and the direct action of conditions does not fall out of those data. The resolvable part is common ancestry of regional biotas, not the mechanism of their differences.

operationalization: Compare morphological or genetic divergence of species that entered an isolated region together, as an already competing set, with divergence of species that arrived alone into new biotic relationships. The claim predicts little change in the first case and more change in the second.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Branch lengths of island and continental clades as a proxy for amount of modification

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Co-occurrence of colonists used to approximate which species arrived into the same biota

obstacles: Whether colonists arrived together or alone is rarely recorded in a database.
Time since arrival and population size vary with isolation and can produce the same divergence pattern.
Relevant comparisons are spread across separate phylogeographic studies.
rationale: The contrast between a co-immigrating assemblage and a singleton colonist is a real comparative prediction, but the arrival mode is not a column in open databases. Trees and ranges support case studies of a few radiations. They do not separate isolation from the other variables that change on islands, so discriminating power stays low.

operationalization: Compute the share of families and genera confined to one biogeographic region, and test whether genera whose species are phylogenetically closest have smaller ranges than genera whose species are loosely related. Widespread tightly knit genera as the rule would refute the second clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Geographic ranges of genera and families

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic membership used to tally endemism by rank

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Relatedness among species within genera, as a stand-in for most natural

obstacles: Most natural has to be translated into monophyly and short internal branches.
Wide-ranging genera are easier to name and sample, which can bias the range-relatedness correlation.
rationale: Endemism by taxonomic rank is directly countable from open catalogues and occurrences. Phylogenetic tightness of genera is available for a large share of plants and vertebrates, which is enough to test the correlation with range. Sampling bias toward widespread taxa is a known confound and can be reduced by using well-studied classes only.

operationalization: For species with range-wide genetic sampling, ask whether gene trees fit one ancestral area followed by spread, or require two or more unrelated origins. A substantial share of species with well-supported multiple origins would challenge the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Georeferenced sequences for phylogeographic origin counts

candidate_datasets.name: BOLD Systems
candidate_datasets.role: Barcode records with locality for single-origin versus multiple-origin tests

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Full geographic ranges against which sampling gaps are judged

obstacles: Range-wide sequences exist for a small fraction of species.
Cryptic species and over-lumped names can look like multiple origins of one species.
Published phylogeographies would have to be compiled, which is months of work at global scope.
rationale: Single versus multiple origin is a standard phylogeographic hypothesis, and public sequences exist for thousands of species. That is a large subset and far from all species. Where sampling is dense, multiple unrelated origins are distinguishable from spread of one population, so the limit is coverage and compilation time.

operationalization: Using late Cenozoic plate reconstructions, bathymetry, and sea-level history, test whether now-separate continents, and those continents and oceanic islands, were joined by continuous dry land during the lifetime of extant species. Sustained land connections among them would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: EarthByte
candidate_datasets.role: Late Cenozoic plate and shoreline reconstructions

candidate_datasets.name: GEBCO
candidate_datasets.role: Bathymetry used with sea-level change to test possible land bridges

obstacles: Almost continuously and the period of existing species need explicit time bounds.
Short-lived bridges have to be scored separately from permanent unions.
Classifying an island as oceanic, rather than a continental fragment, is a geological judgment.
rationale: Bathymetry and plate reconstructions directly record whether dry land connected today's separate continents and oceanic islands in the late Cenozoic. The continuous-union reading is decidable for the major continents and for true oceanic islands. Ambiguity is confined to intermittent bridges and to islands of disputed crustal type.

operationalization: Estimate the fraction of species in a regional flora whose dried seeds stay buoyant and then germinate after a seawater exposure long enough to cross about 900 miles. A flora-scale fraction far from one tenth, under that protocol, would refute the numerical claim.

candidate_datasets.name: LEDA Traitbase
candidate_datasets.role: Seed buoyancy measurements for northwest European species, as a partial experimental sample

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Seed mass and dispersal traits used as a weak proxy for drift potential

obstacles: No public dataset applies one seawater flotation and germination protocol to a whole flora.
Available buoyancy trials often use fresh water and omit germination after drying.
Transit time for 900 miles depends on a current speed the claim leaves implicit.
rationale: The fraction that survives a stated ocean crossing is a sharp numerical target. Existing trait databases cover buoyancy or seed morphology for some floras and do not contain the seawater-plus-germination trial at flora scale. A compiled subset of published experiments can bound the fraction for particular coasts and cannot confirm the one-tenth figure for a flora in general.

operationalization: Plot floristic similarity against ocean distance and ask whether similarity remains appreciable over a few hundred miles, including continent-to-nearby-island gaps, and falls to the level seen between distant continents. Ready floristic exchange between distant continents would count against the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Regional and island plant checklists for similarity versus isolation

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence records used to fill gaps between published floras

obstacles: Ancient land connections and human transport can produce the same distance decay.
Currents, birds, driftwood, and ice are bundled together and are not separate variables in flora data.
rationale: Floristic similarity against sea distance is computable from open checklists and can show whether distant continents are more distinct than nearby island gaps. That pattern is compatible with occasional short-range transport and also with old geology and trade. The data resolve the biogeographic outcome more readily than which means of transport produced it.

operationalization: For arctic-alpine species shared among separated mountains and the Arctic, test whether last-glacial fossils occur in the intervening lowlands and whether genetic data show one recent northern population. Deep divergence among summit populations, together with no glacial-age lowland fossils, would count against a glacial-relict origin.

candidate_datasets.name: Neotoma Paleoecology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Last-glacial pollen and plant remains from lowlands between present alpine stations

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Modern arctic and alpine ranges of the candidate species

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Sequences comparing summit and arctic populations of the same species

obstacles: Pollen and many macrofossils are not identified to species.
Range-wide genetic studies cover a subset of the European and North American biota.
Survival on unglaciated peaks and later long-distance dispersal can mimic parts of the relict pattern.
rationale: Glacial-age lowland fossils and modern ranges are in open databases and can test the geographic half of the relict hypothesis for many plants. Species-level identity of fossils and the genetic unity of summit populations are available only case by case. The full claim is decidable for well-studied European and North American taxa and not for the whole arctic-alpine biota.

operationalization: Estimate divergence times and ancestral areas for temperate clades shared by North America and Europe, and check Pliocene fossils from Arctic landmasses. Divergences much older than the Pliocene, or no northern fossil connection, would count against this history.

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: Published divergence times for shared temperate clades

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Pliocene and Pleistocene fossils from high northern latitudes

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Living temperate ranges in North America and Europe

obstacles: Clock dates for the same clade often span more than the Pliocene.
A Beringian route and a North Atlantic route both fit a circumpolar source.
Very little identity has no sharp similarity threshold.
rationale: Relatedness of the two temperate biotas, northern fossils, and rough divergence times are all in public compilations. The specific Pliocene timing and a single circumpolar source are softer, because date errors are wide and more than one northern route fits the same trees. The analysis can support or weaken the outline for many clades and not pin down the historical detail.

operationalization: Compare independently dated temperature proxies and glacial maxima across latitudes through the last glacial cycle. Cold intervals offset by a large part of the cycle would refute worldwide simultaneity; overlap within a few thousand years would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA Paleoclimatology
candidate_datasets.role: Ice-core, marine, and terrestrial temperature and glacier records for the last glacial cycle

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
candidate_datasets.role: Dated paleoclimate series used to compare regions on one timescale

obstacles: Orbital tuning of marine cores builds in some of the synchrony under test.
Tropical and some southern land records are sparser than the polar ice cores.
At least in part simultaneous can be met by a weak overlap.
rationale: Global proxy compilations already align last-glacial temperature and ice extent on shared age models. A small team can compare the timing of maxima by latitude with standard age-depth data. Tuning and uneven tropical coverage limit precision, and they leave a clear test of whether the cold interval was broadly shared.

operationalization: Compare species identity and phylogenetic relatedness among temperate lowland floras and high-mountain floras, including tropical mountains, with relatedness of those floras to tropical lowlands. Mountain and temperate floras that are generally unrelated would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Alpine and lowland plant checklists for shared and related species

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence records of temperate and mountain plants worldwide

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic distance among species that are not identical

obstacles: Tropical alpine inventories and DNA coverage are thinner than European mountain floras.
Closely related needs a fixed rank or a phylogenetic-distance cutoff.
rationale: Checklist and occurrence data can count shared species and shared genera between mountain and temperate floras worldwide. Phylogenetic distance covers the distinct-but-allied clause for a large fraction of seed plants. Tropical mountains are the weak geographic slice, and the temperate and northern-alpine comparison is already well populated.

operationalization: For plant clades disjunct between the hemispheres, infer dispersal direction from ancestral-area reconstruction and test whether north-to-south events predominate. Counts of direction do not by themselves show that natural selection on a larger northern land area caused the asymmetry.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Hemispheric ranges of disjunct plant clades

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Trees used for ancestral-area direction of dispersal

obstacles: Ancestral-area results move when extinction or northern sampling bias is modeled differently.
Direction of spread does not measure dominating power or demonstrate selection.
Amphitropical clades have been studied one at a time and are not one analysis-ready table.
rationale: A predominance of north-to-south events is inferable for clades that already have trees and range data, which is a subset of southern disjunct plants. The selective-dominance explanation is an extra causal claim those reconstructions do not decide. Compilation and sensitivity to sampling keep the directional test partial.

operationalization: Count naturalized European species established in the Río de la Plata region and in Australia, and naturalized southern-hemisphere species established in Europe. A symmetric exchange, or a surplus of southern species in Europe, would refute the asymmetry.

candidate_datasets.name: GloNAF
candidate_datasets.role: Lists of naturalized alien plant species by recipient region and native origin

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence records flagged as introduced, including animals that plant lists omit

obstacles: Colonial trade and propagule pressure favor European sources regardless of any intrinsic dominance.
Recording has been more intense for European weeds than for southern plants arriving in Europe.
Animal naturalizations are less completely compiled than plants.
rationale: Naturalized floras with native ranges are tabulated in an open global database, so the Europe-to-south versus south-to-Europe counts are a direct query. Animals can be added from occurrence flags with more cleaning. Propagule pressure explains the asymmetry and does not prevent counting it.

operationalization: Combine pre-glacial Antarctic fossil plants with phylogenies of southern-hemisphere disjunct genera and ask whether those genera connect through an Antarctic source older than the glacial period. Roots centered only on Australia or South America, with no Antarctic fossil link, would count against the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Antarctic plant fossils from warmer pre-glacial intervals

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Living ranges of southern disjunct genera

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Relationships among the southern members of those genera

obstacles: The Antarctic macrofossil flora is small and geographically narrow.
Continental breakup, later dispersal, and an Antarctic source are hard to separate when divergence dates are uncertain.
rationale: Antarctic fossils and southern ranges exist in public databases, and trees exist for many of the classic disjunct genera. Together they can test an Antarctic connection for a subset of genera. Date uncertainty and the thin fossil flora leave continental breakup and overseas dispersal as live alternatives for most clades.

operationalization: Compare geographic range sizes of freshwater species with those of related terrestrial species, and measure how often freshwater genera occur on more than one continent. Ranges no larger than terrestrial relatives, and regionally restricted freshwater allies, would count against the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrences of freshwater plants, insects, molluscs, and other groups

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Freshwater fish ranges as one well-coded class inside the broader claim

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomy and distribution context for freshwater molluscs and other aquatic invertebrates

obstacles: Habitat is poorly coded on many occurrence records, so freshwater sets need extra filtering.
Cryptic species divide ranges that look cosmopolitan under older names.
Enormous needs a comparison group, because there is no absolute range cutoff.
rationale: Range size and cross-continental genus occupancy are computable for fishes and for several invertebrate and plant groups from open sources. Habitat mislabels and cryptic diversity reduce coverage below the full set of freshwater classes. A comparison with terrestrial relatives in the same clades is still a direct and feasible test of the wide-range pattern.

operationalization: Intersect native freshwater fish lists among continents, and measure how species are shared among river basins within a continent. One documented native species on two distant continents would refute the never clause; consistent sharing of whole faunas between neighbouring basins would challenge the irregular within-continent pattern.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Native freshwater fish distributions by country, basin, and continent

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Independent occurrence records used to check FishBase range statements

obstacles: Introduced populations have to be removed, and status flags are sometimes wrong.
Distant continents need an explicit list, because neighbouring landmasses exchanged fish across recent land connections.
rationale: Freshwater fish ranges are among the best-coded biogeographic datasets, and both a global checklist and occurrence records are public. Presence of the same native species on two distant continents is a single-counterexample test. Within-continent basin overlap is the same data aggregated one level down, so both clauses can be scored together.

operationalization: Relate the genetic connectivity of widespread freshwater plants and small invertebrates to waterbird flyways, and compare documented bird transport of their seeds and eggs with transport by wind or water. Connectivity that follows bird movements more closely than other vectors would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: eBird
candidate_datasets.role: Waterbird movements and flyways as the proposed dispersal network

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Ranges of freshwater plants and invertebrates to compare with those flyways

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Population-genetic data for connectivity along proposed bird routes

obstacles: Transport experiments and vector comparisons are scattered in papers and are not one database.
People move aquatic organisms widely, which can create the same ranges.
Mainly requires a quantitative ranking of vectors that existing data rarely provide.
rationale: Bird movements and aquatic ranges are public, and some genetic studies line up with flyways, so a partial association test is possible. The causal ranking of birds over water, wind, and people is not in those databases. The mechanism can be examined for a handful of plants and microcrustaceans and not shown to be the main process worldwide.

operationalization: Compare native species richness of oceanic islands with continental areas of equal size, with climate included as a covariate. Equal richness once area and climate are matched would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Island and mainland plant species counts on a common area basis

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Vertebrate and other occurrence-based richness for islands and continents

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim
candidate_datasets.role: Climate covariates so physical conditions are held roughly constant

obstacles: Inventories are far more complete for plants and vertebrates than for insects.
Results depend on excluding continental islands that were once connected to mainlands.
Occurrence density differs sharply among islands.
rationale: Species-area comparisons with a climate covariate are a standard analysis of open flora checklists and occurrence data. Plants and land vertebrates match the claim's scope well enough for a clear island-versus-continent contrast. Invertebrates remain under-catalogued, which limits the phrase all kinds and does not block the test for the groups with inventories.

operationalization: For oceanic islands, compute the proportion of species found nowhere else and compare that proportion with mainland regions of similar area. Endemism no higher than on continents, after inventory completeness is taken into account, would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Island flora checklists with endemic status and area

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Global ranges used to check whether island species occur anywhere else

obstacles: Single-island endemics are sensitive to taxonomic splitting and to undersampling of neighbouring islands.
Insects, where endemism may be highest, are the least completely listed.
A raw percentage has to be judged against a species-area baseline.
rationale: Endemism fractions for island plants are already coded in open flora inventories, and occurrence data can audit whether a species is truly absent elsewhere. Vertebrate islands are similarly tractable. The test is weaker for insects and for tiny islets with incomplete lists, which is a coverage limit inside an otherwise direct comparison.

operationalization: On the same islands, compare percent endemism among groups ordered by a dispersal measure that is independent of endemism, such as a marine habit or sustained flight. High endemism in the groups that arrive most readily would count against the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Island occurrences of land birds, seabirds, and other groups used to compute endemism

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: Marine mollusc distributions for a low-modification comparison group

obstacles: Inferring ease of arrival from endemism itself would make the test circular.
Independent dispersal traits are available for birds and incomplete for shells and insects.
Arrival in a body versus arrival as scattered individuals is seldom recorded.
rationale: Endemism by group on the same islands is computable from checklists, and a marine-versus-terrestrial contrast supplies a dispersal axis that is not defined by the endemism figures. The in-a-body clause and the finer ranking of arrival ability are not in those data. The test works for a few dispersal classes and stays confounded for the rest.

operationalization: Compare growth form of island endemics with their closest mainland relatives and ask whether shifts from herb to shrub or tree are concentrated on oceanic islands that lacked tree colonists in that clade. Woodiness that arrived already evolved on the mainland would fail the in-situ selection scenario.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Woodiness and growth form of island and mainland species

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Island floras linked to growth-form traits

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Sister-group relationships used to tell in-situ change from arrival of already woody plants

obstacles: Ancestral growth form and sister-species pairs are not stored as one global analysis table.
Woody colonists establishing more easily than herbs imitates evolution of woodiness after arrival.
The selection mechanism is stronger than the woodiness pattern alone.
rationale: Island woodiness relative to mainland relatives is recoverable from trait databases and floras for many clades. Separating colonization by woody lineages from change after arrival needs a tree and is only partly assembled. The adaptive story about stature under selection is an interpretation of that pattern, so the data resolve the comparative prediction more than the mechanism.

operationalization: List oceanic islands, set aside continental fragments and recorded introductions, and test whether any native frog, toad, or newt is present. A native amphibian on a clearly oceanic island would refute universal natural absence.

candidate_datasets.name: AmphibiaWeb
candidate_datasets.role: Native amphibian distributions, including island occurrences and introductions

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Independent occurrence records for island amphibians

obstacles: Some Pacific islands sit on arcs or fragments whose oceanic status is disputed.
Introduced frogs are now widespread and have to be separated from native status.
rationale: Native amphibian presence on islands is a presence-absence question with two open distribution sources. Geological classification of islands is available from the same plate and bathymetric data used elsewhere and is the main judgment call. A single confirmed native population on a never-connected oceanic island decides the universal wording.

operationalization: Measure each island's minimum distance to a continent or large continental island and record whether it has a native non-flying terrestrial mammal. A confirmed native land mammal beyond about 300 miles would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: Native non-volant mammal lists by island

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence records used to check island mammal status

candidate_datasets.name: GEBCO
candidate_datasets.role: Bathymetry and shoreline geography for distance to the nearest continent

obstacles: The result depends on what counts as a great continental island and on using over-water distance.
A few island mammals have disputed native status or may have arrived with people.
rationale: Island mammal lists and shoreline geography are public, and the 300-mile threshold is an explicit cutoff. Excluding bats and domestic animals matches the claim's own scope. Disputed native status affects a handful of cases and can be treated as a sensitivity check around an otherwise direct test.

operationalization: Score bat presence, and the fraction of bat species endemic to the island, across oceanic islands ordered by isolation. Absence of bats from most remote islands, or no rise in endemism with isolation, would count against the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: Island bat lists and endemic species

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Bat occurrences used to audit presence on islands missing from checklists

obstacles: Small islands are poorly surveyed for bats, so absence is weaker evidence than presence.
Almost every island needs a minimum size, because tiny islets are poor bat habitat.
Endemism depends on whether island populations are ranked as species.
rationale: Bat checklists for islands and archipelagos are public and can be joined to isolation distance. Presence on remote islands and the endemism of those bats are both countable, with a pre-set size cutoff to make almost every operational. Undersurvey of the smallest islets limits absence claims and does not block the test for islands large enough to have been searched.
